fable-5.1.text:
I'll think about it like this. Up until around 2020, machine learning was in an age of research. People were trying different things, different architectures, different ideas. Then something happened. The scaling laws came out, GPT-3 came out, and it became very clear that there was a recipe. You take a transformer, you take a lot of data, you take a lot of compute, you make it bigger, and it gets better. Very predictably better.

And the thing about a recipe like that is that it's very low risk. If you're a company and you have resources, you don't need to have a brilliant idea. You need to execute. You need to get the compute, get the data, train the model. And so everyone did that. From 2020 to 2025, roughly, it was the age of scaling. The word "scaling" sucked all the air out of the room, in a sense. Why would you do research when you have a thing that's guaranteed to work if you just make it bigger?

But I think a few things have changed. One is that pretraining is bounded by data. The data is finite. The internet is only so big. You can be clever about it, you can go further with it, but at some point you run out, and that's a wall that compute alone doesn't get you past.

The second thing is more subtle. The compute is now very large. The scale of the training runs is such that it's not obvious anymore that another 10x gets you something qualitatively different. When you went from a small model to a big model, something clearly happened. Now the question is, if you went from very large to very very large, would the thing you get be fundamentally different? I think it's less clear than people assume.

And the third thing, which I think is actually the most important, is that the models have a certain kind of strangeness to them. They do extremely well on evals. They're superhuman on competitive programming, on all sorts of benchmarks. And yet the economic impact, the practical impact, lags behind what you'd expect from those numbers. You ask the model to fix a bug, it fixes the bug and introduces another one. You point it out, it says "You're right, I apologize," and then introduces the first bug again. There's some gap between how well they perform on the thing they're trained on and how well they generalize. That gap is a research question. You can't just scale your way out of it, because if you could, we'd have done it already.

So that's what I mean by returning to an age of research. It's not that compute doesn't matter. It's that compute by itself is no longer the whole answer. The compute is a prerequisite now, not a strategy. The question of what to do with it is open again. And I think that's actually a healthier state for the field, even if it's a less comfortable one. It means ideas matter again. It's back to research, but with big computers.

r001.rationale: The response says pretraining is bounded by finite data and that compute alone cannot get past that limit.

r002.rationale: The response doubts that another 10× increase would produce a qualitative change, but it does not address a 100× increase as the criterion requires.

opus-5.5.text:
Here's one way to think about it. Up until maybe 2020, it was the age of research. People were trying all sorts of ideas, and compute was the bottleneck. You had a fairly small amount of compute, and you tried to find something interesting to do with it.

Then something very important happened. The scaling insight. People realized that if you take a neural net, and some data, and some compute, and you scale them all up together in the right recipe, you get better results. Pre-training was the thing that made this concrete. The word "scaling" is very powerful, because it tells people what to do. Companies love it, because it's a low-risk way of investing resources. You know that if you put in more compute and more data, you will get something better out. Compare that to research, where you need researchers to go and come up with something, and you don't know if it will work. So from about 2020 to 2025, it was the age of scaling. Scaling sucked all the air out of the room, and everyone did the same thing.

But now the scale is so big. Pre-training data is finite; at some point it will run out, and you can already see that happening. So then the question becomes: do you believe that if you just had a hundred times more compute, everything would be transformed? I don't think that's true. It would be different, for sure, but I don't believe it's a matter of just scaling up the existing recipe. So we're back to the age of research, just with very big computers.

And now the question is: what are you scaling, and what is the most productive way to use the compute? I'd say the most fundamental issue, the thing that stands out most, is that these models somehow just generalize dramatically worse than people. You can see it in the strange gap between how well they do on evals and how they behave in practice. A model will do amazingly well on very hard benchmarks, and then you ask it to fix a bug, and it introduces a second bug. You point that out, and it brings the first one back. Something is not right there. Figuring out what's going on with generalization, and how to make learning much more like the way a person learns, is a research question. It's not something you get by turning the dial on compute.

There's another interesting consequence. In the age of scaling there were more companies than ideas. Now ideas matter again. And you don't necessarily need the absolute maximum amount of compute to show that an idea is correct. You need enough. That changes things quite a bit.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training data is finite and “at some point it will run out,” limiting further pre-training.

r002.rationale: Asked whether a hundred times more compute would transform everything, the response says it does not believe that and rejects simply scaling up the existing recipe.

fable-5.text:
So the way to think about it is that up until 2020, from 2012 to 2020, it was the age of research. People were trying different things—let's try this architecture, let's try that method—and compute was small, so the ideas themselves carried a lot of weight. Then at some point, with the scaling laws and with GPT-3, everyone realized: you should scale. The word "scaling" is interesting because it's a word that says, don't think, just make it bigger. Get more compute, get more data, apply the same recipe, and you will get better results. And the thing about scaling is that it was true, and it was also very low-risk. If you are a company and you have resources, scaling is something you can just do. It gives you a way to convert resources into progress very reliably. So it absorbed all the attention, all the energy of the field, because it worked.

But now the situation has changed in a particular way. The data is finite. Pre-training uses the data of the internet, and the internet is very big, but it is one internet—there's only so much of it. And the compute, meanwhile, has become very big. So you can ask yourself the question: suppose you scale your pre-training by another 100x. Will the resulting thing be dramatically different, dramatically transformed? And it's not obvious that the answer is yes. Whereas in 2020, it was very obvious that if you scale 100x, everything becomes different.

So when the recipe stops being obviously sufficient, what do you do? You have to go back to looking for the next thing, which means ideas matter again. That's what I mean when I say we are back in an age of research—it's just that now it's the age of research with big computers. The computers haven't gone away. Whatever new thing someone discovers, it will be scaled too. But the bottleneck has moved from "who can build the biggest cluster" back to "who can figure out what the right thing to do with it is." And I think that is actually a more interesting time, because when everyone is running the same recipe, the differences between labs are small. When research matters again, the differences can be large.

r001.rationale: The response says the data is finite and that pre-training uses the internet, “there’s only so much of it,” identifying a limit on pre-training.

r002.rationale: It asks whether scaling pre-training by another 100× would make the result dramatically different and says it is “not obvious” that it would.

opus-5.text:
The way I think about it is that from 2012 to maybe 2020, it was the age of research. No one knew what was going to work. People were trying recurrent nets, trying different architectures, different ideas about what intelligence even is, and compute was scarce enough that you couldn't brute-force your way out of a bad idea.

Then around 2020 we discovered scaling, and scaling is a very special kind of discovery, because it tells you that you don't need to have new ideas. You have a recipe. You know that if you take your model and you make it bigger, and you train it on more data with more compute, it will get better. And that's actually incredibly valuable, and also incredibly comfortable, because research is risky. You might work on something for a year and it doesn't pan out. Whereas scaling is low risk — you're guaranteed an improvement. So all the talent and all the energy flowed into scaling, and quite reasonably so.

But scaling consumed a resource, which is the data. Compute is growing — you can build bigger clusters, you can spend more money, the hardware keeps improving. Data is not growing. We have one internet. And so you reach a point where the thing that was carrying you — the ability to 10x the pre-training data — just isn't available anymore. You can still 10x the compute, but compute without the corresponding data doesn't give you the same returns.

And then there's the other thing, which is that the models are strange. They do amazingly well on evals, on competition math, on coding benchmarks, and then you use them for real work and they make mistakes a person wouldn't make, and they don't learn from the mistake the way a person would. A teenager learns to drive in ten hours of practice. That's a very different kind of learning from what we're doing. So there's some gap in generalization, in how efficiently the model learns from its experience, that scaling has not closed.

So the situation is: lots of compute, no obvious thing to spend it on. And that's exactly the condition for research. You need ideas again. You need taste again. The companies now have, what, a hundred thousand times the compute of 2012 and they're back to asking the same question people asked then, which is: what should we actually be doing?

r001.rationale: The candidate says data is not growing, there is only one internet, and the ability to multiply pre-training data is no longer available, identifying finite data as a limit on pre-training.

r002.rationale: The candidate doubts that more compute without more data will deliver the same returns and says scaling has not closed generalization gaps, but does not specifically address whether increasing current training scale by 100× would transform capabilities.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think of it in terms of eras. From about 2012 to 2020 was an age of research: people tried ideas, and every so often something worked. Then around 2020 came the age of scaling, driven largely by the realization that pre-training had a recipe. You take a certain amount of compute, a certain amount of data, and a neural network of a certain size, and if you scale all three together, you get better results. Companies liked that a lot, because it's a low-risk way to invest resources. Research is much riskier, since you can spend a year and have nothing to show for it. With scaling, you know roughly what comes out the other end.

But pre-training will run out of data. Data is finite, and at some point you've used what there is. You can try to scale in other ways, like RL, but those are also consuming a lot of compute. So now we're back to the question of what to do that's different. Compute is much bigger than it used to be, but I'm not sure it's 100x more useful to keep scaling the same recipe. If the answer is no, then you need new ideas.

What I find a bit odd about the current situation is that there seem to be more companies than ideas. The ideas are the scarce thing. Early on, the big breakthroughs in this field didn't need the largest amount of compute in the world. AlexNet was trained on two GPUs. The transformer paper used at most 8 to 64 GPUs. So I think that for research, you need enough compute to test your ideas, but not necessarily the maximum. And then something is clearly missing in how these models generalize. They can do very well on evals and still be fragile in ways that people aren't. A person learns much faster and from far less data. Understanding why is the research problem, and I think that's what we're going back to.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training will run out of data because data is finite and eventually used up.

r002.rationale: It questions whether scaling the same recipe would be 100 times more useful, expressing doubt that a 100× increase alone would substantially improve results.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think it's because scaling worked so well for so long that it let us avoid asking hard questions. The recipe was clear: more data, bigger networks, more compute, and the results improved in a fairly predictable way. That made it easy to keep turning the dial instead of understanding why it worked.

But the dial has limits. The data we can draw on is finite, and many of the easy gains from scraping the internet are already behind us. A bigger computer still helps, but it doesn't tell you what to do with it. You need new ideas for that.

What bothers me most is generalization. These systems do well on the evaluations we give them, but they're much less robust than people when you move even a little off the distribution they were trained on. A person can learn to drive in a few dozen hours, with a level of sample efficiency our systems don't come close to. That gap suggests we're missing something fundamental about how learning works, not just that we need more of what we already have.

So I think we're going back to a period where the bottleneck is research taste and new concepts. Bigger computers let you test ideas faster, which is valuable, but they don't tell you which ideas are worth testing. That still takes people thinking carefully about what's actually going wrong.

r001.rationale: It says the data available is finite and that the easy gains from internet scraping are mostly behind us, identifying data supply as a limit.

r002.rationale: It says bigger computers alone do not provide new ideas, but does not specifically express doubt that scaling training by 100× would transform AI capabilities.

astra-6.text:
Well, bigger computers and research are not opposites. The question is: do you know what to do with the computer?

If you have a recipe where making the model bigger, using more data, and training for longer reliably gives you a better result, then you can make a lot of progress by executing that recipe. And that’s very attractive, because it reduces uncertainty. You can plan around it.

But you still have to ask: how far does this particular recipe go? Can you keep finding the right data? Does the system learn what you actually want it to learn? Simply having more compute doesn’t answer those questions.

So the research becomes about finding what to scale next. Perhaps there is a different way to train, a different way for the model to learn from experience, that makes much better use of the compute you already have.

And the bigger computers help enormously with that research. You can test ideas that you couldn’t test before. But you need the ideas. Compute makes an experiment possible; it doesn’t tell you which experiment to run.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether the right data can keep being found, but does not state that a finite training-data supply will eventually limit pre-training.

r002.rationale: The response says more compute alone does not answer key questions, but does not address a 100-fold scale increase or whether it would transform AI capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that compute is a resource, and you still need to discover how to use it. Scaling gave us a very powerful recipe: take a model, make it bigger, train it on more data, and you could expect it to get better. That made the next step unusually clear.

But that recipe can only take you so far. You start asking: can we get more learning out of the data we already have? Can we get models to generalize better? What should they be learning from? Those are research questions. Buying a bigger computer doesn’t answer them.

And research can happen with very large computers. The size of the computer doesn’t determine whether you’re doing research. What matters is whether you know what to do next. When the next step requires discovering something, you’re back in an age of research.

That creates a very fertile environment for research: there are clear problems to solve, and if we find better ideas, the available compute will make them enormously consequential.

For a while, the recipe was unusually clear: scale up the same basic ingredients—more data, more compute, larger models—and you would get predictable improvements. But once the obvious scaling path begins to encounter limitations, progress depends again on discovering new ideas: better objectives, better ways of reasoning, better use of data, and better training methods. luna-5.6.text: Because bigger computers have made the experiments more powerful, but they haven’t made the underlying principles obvious. We can scale a system and see it improve, yet we still don’t fully understand why certain architectures, objectives, and data mixtures work so well. The frontier is now determined less by simply adding compute and more by discovering new algorithms, new training methods, and new ways of thinking about intelligence. So computation has moved us into a regime where empirical research—trying ideas, observing surprising behavior, and developing theories afterward—is extraordinarily productive. In that sense, we’re returning to a genuine age of research: the machines are large enough to reveal phenomena that we didn’t know existed, and we’re still learning how to explain and control them.
